units: the heart races and the hands go damp before speaking in front of a group
whoever feels this believes himself fragile and judges himself clumsy
the dread pushes him to avoid meetings where he will have to speak
avoidance strengthens the dread instead of easing it
breathing out more slowly than one breathes in slows the heartbeat
rehearsing the opening sentence aloud at home helps the start
it is better to tolerate the first trembling than to fight it
a relaxed friend can serve as a practice audience
the panic lessens after several repeated attempts
text: You will know the feeling. A group turns towards you, and before a single word comes out the heart is racing and the palms have gone damp. Anyone caught in that state tends to read it as proof of some private weakness, and to write himself off as clumsy. So the meetings where speaking is expected get quietly dodged, and there the trap closes, because every escape feeds the dread rather than starving it. Three plain habits open a way out. Breathe out more slowly than you breathe in, and the heartbeat follows and settles. Say your opening line aloud at home, often enough that the mouth already knows the road. Then let the first shaking happen instead of wrestling with it. A relaxed friend makes a decent practice audience. After enough attempts the panic wears thin, and the nerves become something you can carry.

units: two opposing positions circulate about the place of feelings in a team
the first demands complete restraint and allows nothing but arguments
the second prizes the open expression of anger and of grief
imposed silence sends the unease travelling underground
compulsory restraint makes colleagues quicker to take offence
expression without limit tires those who have to listen
a middle way consists in naming one's state without demanding its repair
this balance sounds obvious to state but calls for slow learning
text: Mention feelings at work and two camps form at once. The first asks for full restraint: the sound professional leaves his moods at the door and puts nothing on the table but arguments. The second prizes the opposite, anger spoken plainly, grief carried in the open in front of everybody. Each side is right about its rival and wrong about itself. Where silence is imposed, the unease does not vanish; it travels underground, and the team grow touchy over remarks that carry no weight. Where everything is poured out, the listeners tire and the meeting turns into a waiting room. What holds is the narrower path between the two: naming what you feel without asking anybody to mend it. To say you are weighed down obliges no colleague to comfort you. Ordinary to state, that distinction is slow to learn.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the listener works in the evening with a headset on a helpline
those who ring keep their anonymity
her voice stays low and never climbs
her first quality is bearing long silences
her second quality is holding on to details given early in the exchange
her third quality is a welcoming tone that promises nothing
one sparing caller took an hour before saying a whole sentence
she will never know what became of those she listened to
text: The voice comes first, low and unhurried, and it never climbs however heavy the line grows. She spends her evenings in a headset on a helpline, taking calls from shaken strangers who give no name at any point. Three skills hold the work together. Patience is the first: she lets silences run on where most of us would rush to fill them. Memory for detail is the second, so that a dog mentioned in the opening minutes comes back from her mouth much later. The third is a warm tone kept clear of familiarity, one that steadies a caller without promising a thing. She tells of a sparing man who took a full hour to produce one complete sentence. What became of him she will never learn. That is the heaviest part of the work: to walk beside people with no sequel, to shelter them for one evening, then to put the receiver down.

units: the programme under review comprises four successive stages
the opening meeting serves to list the triggers of the anxiety
the self-rating scale stays understandable without prior training
the breathing training imposes one identical pace on every participant
this single pace overlooks the differences in lung capacity
graded exposure is the best designed point of the programme
the list of feared situations is drawn up with the patient
the last meeting handles relapse prevention on a single sheet
the final verdict is mixed: rigorous middle, rigid opening, rushed ending
text: Four stages make up the programme under review, and each deserves a verdict of its own. It opens with a structured interview in which the practitioner lists what sets the anxiety off. That part holds up well, since the questions leave room and the self-rating scale stays readable for somebody with no training behind him. The breathing work that follows is harder to defend, because one pace is set for the whole room while lung capacity differs from person to person. Graded exposure, the third stage, is where the design is at its best: the ladder of feared situations is built with the patient rather than handed down. The closing session then disposes of relapse prevention on a single photocopied sheet. The overall picture is uneven, a rigorous middle weakened by a rigid entrance and a rushed way out.

units: the writer writes to explain a long absence never clearly justified
the death of his sister happened a short while ago
the grief did not lessen as he had supposed
the writer became inattentive and forgot his files
he reread the same page without holding on to its content
this scattering damaged the quality of his reports
from it he conceived a sense of being incapable
that sense led him to decline the invitations of his team
his silence was taken for contempt
he is starting therapy and wants to return by stages
text: I am writing to you about my long absence, which I have never explained to you with any clarity. My sister died a short while ago, and the effect it had on me was not the one I had supposed. I thought the grief would settle in and then thin out; it took quite another road. First it made me vague. Files slipped my mind. I would read a page and reach the bottom of it holding nothing at all, not one line of it. My reports lost their quality through that scattering, and out of the poor work grew a sense of being no longer capable. From that sense came avoidance: I stopped answering the invitations my team sent me, and my silence was read as disdain. Seen from your desk, the chain must have looked opaque. I have begun seeing a therapist, and I would like to take my duties up again by stages.

units: the question raised concerns learning to sleep when the mind stirs
insomnia feeds itself through the fear of not sleeping
the long waking then proves that fear right
the first recommendation consists in shortening the time spent in bed
that window is then widened by steps once falling asleep is quick again
it is advised to leave the bed when the night drags on
this instruction avoids tying the bed to a struggle
the effect of screens exists but it is overstated
mental stirring weighs more than screens do
text: Can sleep be learnt, when the mind refuses to switch itself off? The question comes up in consultation after consultation, and the accepted answer starts with something unwelcome. Insomnia keeps itself alive: the fear of not sleeping holds you awake, and the waking hours then prove the fear right. So what is to be done? The first piece of advice sounds wrong, because it asks for less time in bed rather than more. The window is squeezed until falling asleep goes quickly again, then widened step by step. A second question follows. Should you get up when the night drags on? Yes, say the protocols, so that the bed stops standing for a struggle. And screens? Their effect is real but blown out of proportion; a churning mind weighs far heavier. One rule survives: a restless head calms better upright than lying down.

units: the elder brother tells his sister that he does not understand their mother
their mother flares up over a tiny mishap but stays calm at bad news
the sister describes their father as working the other way round
the father falls silent during the crises and turns kind once quiet returns
the mother lets her anger out fast and forgets it fast
the father stores it up and then gives way weeks later
the brother judges the loud manner more wounding because the words land straight
the sister prefers that manner because one knows what to expect
both admit they were handed a model without choosing it
text: The elder brother was telling his sister that their mother made no sense to him. A knocked-over glass and she was shouting, while bad news arrived and she took it steadily. His sister said their father ran the other way round, mute for as long as the crisis lasted, then warm again the moment the house went quiet. One of them lets the anger out fast and forgets it just as fast, she said; the other takes everything in, keeps it, and gives way all at once some weeks on. The brother objected that the loud manner wounds more, since the words land straight in your face. His sister thought the reverse: at least you know where you stand, whereas a long silence leaves you guessing anything you like. They agreed in the end that neither way was better, and that each had been handed a model without ever choosing it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: three readings of mental suffering came before the scientific discipline
these readings piled up rather than replaced one another
the supernatural reading put the disorder down to a force from outside
it healed through ceremonies meant to drive that force out
the reading of inner fluids explained melancholy by an imbalance of the body
it turned to bleeding, to purges and to prescribed diets
the moral reading held the sufferer answerable for his own disorder
it laid down strict hours, work with the hands and separation from others
each reading brought forth its own houses and its own vocabulary
phrases born of these readings survive in everyday speech
text: Long before the mind became a subject of study, mental suffering was read in three ways, and these piled up on one another rather than taking turns. The first was supernatural. Something from outside had entered the sufferer, and the cure lay in ceremonies meant to drive it back out. The second looked inward at the fluids of the body, blaming melancholy on an imbalance there; blood was let, purges were given, diets were laid down. The third was moral. It held the sufferer answerable for his own disorder and put its faith in discipline: fixed hours, work with the hands, separation from others. Each reading built its own houses, its own trades, its own words. Each left deposits in ordinary speech, where a black mood and a possessed mind are still spoken of. Careful clinical observation came later, and took generations to win.

units: the newborn has only three signals of feeling at his disposal
these signals are distress, settling and wide-awake curiosity
towards the end of the first year the fear of unknown faces appears
this fear shows that the child now sorts close ones from strangers
in front of a mirror the child works out at last that the smudge is on his own forehead
from that recognition are born awkwardness, pride and shame
schooling teaches that a feeling can be kept hidden
the child discovers that a soothing face can deceive
in adolescence the charge of feeling grows before the power to hold back
this gap explains how hard the outbursts of that age break
text: Watch a newborn. The whole range comes down to three signals: distress, settling and a wide-awake curiosity. Everything else is built on top of them. Near the end of the first year, unfamiliar faces begin to worry the baby, which shows that familiar people are now sorted from strangers. Then comes the discovery of the self. Put in front of a mirror, the child works out at last that the smudge belongs to his own forehead, and from that discovery come awkwardness, pride and shame. School adds a further layer: a feeling can be kept back, a soothing face may be lying, and tears come less readily with others watching. In adolescence the charge rises while the brakes are still being fitted, which is why the storms of those years break so hard. The whole structure takes decades to finish.

units: an incident on a hospital ward illustrates how a mood spreads
the ward coordinator took a painful piece of family news as her shift began
she informed no colleague of it
her speech sped up and her instructions turned clipped
the team changed its behaviour within two handovers
the exchanges grew shorter and the cross-checks fell away
the number of preparation errors doubled
the later review set aside tiredness and patient numbers as explanations
the cause held to be the silent passing on through posture, gaze and speed of voice
a short debriefing meeting put the coordination back
text: One incident on a hospital ward showed with unusual clarity how a mood spreads from person to person. The nursing coordinator, calm by habit, took a painful piece of family news just as her shift began. She said nothing about it to anybody, yet her speech sped up and her instructions came out clipped. Within two handovers the whole team had shifted: exchanges grew shorter, cross-checks fell away, and the air on the ward turned heavy. The measurable result showed in the incident book, where errors in preparation doubled. The review carried out afterwards set aside tiredness and patient numbers, both of which had held steady. What remained was the silent passing on of a mood through posture, through the eyes, through the speed of a voice. A short meeting to talk it through was enough to put the coordination back.
